'''''Cnidoscolus aconitifolius''''', commonly known as '''chaya''', '''tree spinach''', '''Mayan tree spinach''', or '''spinach tree''', is a large, fast-growing and leafy [[Perennial plant|perennial]] [[shrub]] in the spurge family [[Euphorbiaceae]].

The plant is native to [[Mexico]]. As with most [[Euphorbiaceae|euphorbias]], the plant exudes an irritating, often toxic [[latex]] when damaged. The plant is cultivated in warm climates for its leaves that are cooked and eaten like [[spinach]].

==Description==
The plant can grow up to {{convert|5|m|ft}} tall.<ref name=":0" /> The leaves are [[palmately lobed]] with three or more lobes that are also lobed themselves, and measure {{convert|10|–|30|cm|abbr=on|frac=2}} across depending on the age and variety.

Small white flowers are arranged in a terminal [[panicle]] held well above the surrounding foliage. The ellipsoid seed pods have longitudinal stripes and measure about {{convert|1.5|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}} across; they are green when immature, turning pale yellow to tan and explosively [[Dehiscence (botany)|dehiscing]] on maturity. Mature seed pods are rarely seen on cultivated specimens so they are often [[vegetatively propagated]]; flowers on such specimens are either sterile or seldom produced.<ref name=":0">{{cite web |author=<!-- not stated --> |title=Chaya|url=https://www.adelaide.edu.au/directory/graham.lyons?dsn=directory.file;field=data;id=40377;m=view|website=University of Adelaide|location=Australia |access-date=2025-11-24}}</ref>

=== Similar species ===
As suggested by its Latin name, the species may resemble members of ''[[Aconitum]]''.

== Taxonomy ==
''Cnidoscolus aconitifolius'' subsp. ''aconitifolius'' is [[endemic]] to northern Mexico south to [[Belize]] and [[Guatemala]], and is cultivated in other countries, as far south as [[Peru]], while ''C. aconitifolius'' subsp. ''polyanthus'' <small>([[Ferdinand Albin Pax|Pax]] and [[Käthe Hoffmann|K.Hoffm.]]) Breckon</small> is restricted to a small area in western Mexico.

Plants in the ''Chayamansa'' [[Cultivar group|group]] (syn. ''C. chayamansa'') are the most widely cultivated, lacking [[stinging hair]]s on their leaves. There are four predominant cultivars based on leaf morphology, notably ''Chayamansa'' (the most common), ''Estrella'', ''Picuda'', and ''Redonda''.<ref name="Grubben" />

=== Etymology ===
The [[specific name (botany)|specific epithet]], ''aconitifolius'', refers to the resemblance of the leaves to those of ''Aconitum'' species—another well-known dangerous, even deadly, genus of plants.

== Distribution ==
Chaya is believed to have originated in the [[Yucatán Peninsula]] of southeastern Mexico, through Central America to [[Panama]].<ref name="Grubben" /><ref>{{cite web |author=<!-- not stated --> |title=Cnidoscolus aconitifolius (Mill.) I.M.Johnst. |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:61821-2 |access-date=2025-11-24 |website=Plants of the World Online |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens Kew |location=United Kingdom}}</ref> 

== Cultivation ==
The species is cultivated in warm regions around the world for its edible leaves, including northern [[South America]], tropical [[Africa]], [[Southeast Asia]], and the [[Pacific islands|Pacific]].[[File:Hai Duong Cnidoscolus aconitifolius.jpg|thumb|Young specimen cultivated in Vietnam.]]
Chaya can be grown as a potherb, preferring full sun and a warm climate. It is easy to grow and it suffers little [[insect]] damage. It may be a tender perennial in the United States, but persists in climates such as Florida. It is tolerant of heavy rain and has some [[drought]]. [[plant propagation|Propagation]] is normally by woody [[Plant stem|stem]] [[cutting (plant)|cuttings]] about {{convert|15|–|30|cm|abbr=on|frac=2|in}} long, as seeds are rarely produced. Early growth is slow as roots are slow to develop on the cuttings, so leaves are not harvested until the second year. Thereafter, chaya leaves may be harvested continuously provided that more than 50% of the leaves are removed from the plant, in order to guarantee healthy new plant growth.

A [[USDA]] study in [[Puerto Rico]] reported that higher yields of greens could be obtained with chaya than any other vegetable they had studied. In another study, chaya leaves were found to contain substantially greater amounts of [[nutrients]] than spinach leaves.<ref name="people.umass.edu">{{cite web |author=Dawn Berkelaar |title=CHAYA |url=http://people.umass.edu/psoil370/Syllabus-files/Chaya.pdf |access-date=18 March 2022 |website=People.umass.edu}}</ref>

===Cultivars===
There are four well-known [[cultivars]], ''Chayamansa'', ''Estrella'', ''Picuda'', and ''Redonda''. Cultivars ''Chayamansa'', ''Estrella'', and ''Redonda''  cannot produce [[seed]]s or [[fruit]] due to unviable [[pollen]], while ''Picuda'' and other cultivars can. These cultivars have fewer [[urticating hairs]] compared to other cultivars and the [[wild type]] of the species, and are thus more common in culinary use.<ref name="Cultivar and Phenology">{{cite journal |last1=Vélez-Gavilán |first1=J. |title=Cnidoscolus aconitifolius (chaya) |url=https://www.cabi.org/isc/datasheet/14554#2f2c2871-11e3-42f3-8411-6f0a4b125e2a |website=(Centre for Agriculture and Bioscience International) Invasive Species Compendium |date=2019 |volume=CABI Compendium |article-number=14554 |doi=10.1079/cabicompendium.14554 |access-date=21 June 2021|doi-access=free }}</ref>

== Toxicity ==
The raw leaves contain large quantities of [[toxic plant|toxic]] [[cyanogenic glycosides]], in addition to the irritating sap typical of the [[Euphorbiaceae]] family. Some varieties also have [[stinging hair]]s and require gloves for harvesting. Thorough cooking destroys both the stinging hairs and toxins found in the raw plant. 

Care should be taken to avoid contact between raw plant material and one's [[mucous membrane]]s including the mouth, eyes, genitals, nose, inner ears, or any otherwise open wound or injury. Complications can occur, from mild irritation to severe burning pain and in more serious cases, temporary blindness if it enters the eyes, or a temporary loss of smell or taste if it touches the nose or mouth. 

While raw consumption is discouraged, some sources state that no more than five raw leaves can be eaten per day. However, to avoid the risk of poisoning, leaves must be cooked for 5–15 minutes before eating, with 20 minutes being recommended most often in recipes.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Grubben |first1=G. J. H. |url=https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_6jrlyOPfr24C |title=Vegetables |publisher=PROTA |year=2004 |isbn=978-90-5782-147-9 |page=[https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_6jrlyOPfr24C/page/n200 200] |quote=chaya.}}</ref><ref name="people.umass.edu" /><ref name="Miracles">{{cite web |title=Nature's Solution to Malnutrition |url=http://miraclesinaction.org/wp-content/uploads/2012/06/Chaya_broch_eng_r2.pdf |access-date=18 March 2022 |website=Miraclesinaction.org}}</ref>  Additionally, aluminum utensils should not be used to cook chaya, as there is a risk of the plant's toxins reacting with aluminum, making the dish unsafe to eat.<ref name="Miracles" /><ref name="Jensen" />

== Uses ==
It is a popular [[leaf vegetable]] in some regional [[Mexican cuisine|Mexican]] and other [[Latin American cuisine|Central American cuisine]]s, used similarly to cooked [[Swiss chard]] or [[spinach]]. Young leaves and the tender stem tips can be eaten boiled, steamed or stir-fried, and has a mild, sometimes [[umami]] taste with a distinct crunchy texture that is retained after cooking.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hutasingh|first1=Nuti|last2=Tubtimrattana|first2=Apinya|last3=Pongpamorn|first3=Pornkanok|last4=Pewlong|first4=Putthamas|last5=Paemanee|first5=Atchara|last6=Tansrisawad|first6=Nat|last7=Siripatrawan|first7=Ubonrat|last8=Sirikantaramas|first8=Supaart|date=2024-07-15|title=Unraveling the effects of drying techniques on chaya leaves: Metabolomics analysis of nonvolatile and volatile metabolites, umami taste, and antioxidant capacity|journal=Food Chemistry|volume=446|article-number=138769 |doi=10.1016/j.foodchem.2024.138769 |pmid=38422636 }}</ref>

[[File:Cnidoscolus chayamansa2 ies.jpg|thumb|right|Chaya leaf]]
Chaya is one of the most productive green vegetables.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.echotech.org/technical/az/aztext/azch2veg.htm#Chay |title=Vegetables and Small Fruits in the Tropics |access-date=10 July 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090307091224/http://www.echotech.org/technical/az/aztext/azch2veg.htm#Chay |archive-date=7 March 2009 }}</ref><ref name="nzdl.sadl.uleth.ca">{{cite web|url=http://nzdl.sadl.uleth.ca/cgi-bin/library?e=d-00000-00---off-0hdl--00-0--0-10-0--0-0---0prompt-10---4------4-0-1l--11-en-50-0--20-about--100-0-1-00-0-0-11-1-0utfZz-8-00-0-1-00-0-0-11-1-0utfZz-8-00&a=d&c=hdl&cl=CL3.10&d=HASH01db635e6cefb81dc6e76991.24.3|title=The nutritive value of chaya, one of the most productive green vegetables|work=Ideas for growing food under difficult conditions - From Amaranth to Zai Holes - ECHO / ECHO development notes|issue=53|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110706211114/http://nzdl.sadl.uleth.ca/cgi-bin/library?e=d-00000-00---off-0hdl--00-0--0-10-0--0-0---0prompt-10---4------4-0-1l--11-en-50-0--20-about--100-0-1-00-0-0-11-1-0utfZz-8-00-0-1-00-0-0-11-1-0utfZz-8-00&a=d&c=hdl&cl=CL3.10&d=HASH01db635e6cefb81dc6e76991.24.3|archive-date=6 July 2011}}</ref> It is rich in [[protein]], [[vitamin]]s, [[calcium]], [[iron]], and [[antioxidant]]s, containing two to three times more nutrients than other, more common leafy vegetables.<ref name="Kuti">{{cite journal |url=http://www.hort.purdue.edu/newcrop/proceedings1996/V3-516.html |first1=Joseph O. |last1=Kuti |first2=Eliseo S. |last2=Torres |title=Potential nutritional and health benefits of tree spinach |pages=516–520 |editor=J. Janick |journal=Progress in New Crops |year=1996}}</ref><ref name="Jensen">{{cite web |url=http://www.mexconnect.com/articles/982-chaya-the-maya-miracle-plant |title=Chaya, the Maya miracle plant |publisher=Mexconnect |date=October 2009 |access-date=2011-05-31}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Kuti | first1 = J. O. | last2 = Konuru | first2 = H. B. | doi = 10.1021/jf030246y | title = Antioxidant Capacity and Phenolic Content in Leaf Extracts of Tree Spinach (''Cnidoscolus'' spp.) | journal = Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry | volume = 52 | issue = 1 | pages = 117–21 | year = 2004 | pmid =  14709023 | bibcode = 2004JAFC...52..117K }}</ref> Cooking is essential prior to consumption because raw chaya leaves contain toxic [[cyanogenic glycosides]], similar to the related crop [[cassava]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://edis.ifas.ufl.edu/MV045|author=James M Stephens|publisher=University of Florida IFAS Extension|title=Chaya – Cnidoscolus chayamansa McVaugh |date=29 October 2018 }}</ref> Aluminum utensils should not be used to cook chaya to avoid possible dangerous side-effects.<ref name="Miracles"/><ref name="Jensen"/>

Traditionally, leaves are simmered for 20 minutes and then served with oil or butter. The stock or liquid in which the leaves are cooked is safe for consumption, as heat causes the [[cyanogenic glycosides]] to decompose, releasing [[hydrogen cyanide]] into the air.<ref name="Jensen"/>

In Mayan traditional medicine, an infusion of the leaves is used to treat kidney stones, high blood pressure, and diabetes.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Guevara-Cruz|first1=Martha|last2=Medina-Vera|first2=Isabel|last3=Cu-Cañetas|first3=Trinidad Eugenia|last4=Cordero-Chan|first4=Yusef 4|last5=Torres|first5=Nimbe |last6=Tovar|first6=Armando R|last7=Márquez-Mota|first7=Claudia|last8=Talamantes-Gómez|first8=José Moisés|last9=Pérez-Monter|first9=Carlos|last10=Lugo|first10=Roberto|last11=Gutiérrez-Solis|first11=Ana Ligia|last12=Avila-Nava|first12=Azalia|date=2021-07-23|title=Chaya Leaf Decreased Triglycerides and Improved Oxidative Stress in Subjects With Dyslipidemia|journal=Frontiers in Nutrition|volume=8|issue=2021|article-number=666243 |publisher=Frontiers|doi=10.3389/fnut.2021.666243 |pmid=34368206 |pmc=8343181 |doi-access=free }}</ref> Experiments with rabbits suggest that chaya leaves have a possible [[antidiabetic]] effect.<ref name="Kuti"/>
